title: India Scraps Six-Month Stay Requirement for OCI Card Applications, Introduces Digital e-OCI System
excerpt: The Ministry of Home Affairs has overhauled Overseas Citizen of India rules for the first time in over a decade, removing a major bureaucratic hurdle while adding new compliance requirements for passport updates.
body:
• India's Ministry of Home Affairs has removed the mandatory six-month continuous stay requirement for OCI card applications filed within India, effective April 8, 2026.
  • A new fee structure sets fresh OCI applications at $275 outside India and ₹15,000 within India, with significantly reduced fees for reissuance and passport updates.
  • OCI cardholders must now update their passport details on the OCI portal within three months of receiving a new passport or face a $25 penalty.
  • India has introduced an electronic OCI (e-OCI) option, making the physical card optional and enabling faster immigration processing through biometric e-gate systems at Indian airports.

The Biggest OCI Overhaul in a Decade

The Ministry of Home Affairs has enacted the most significant revision to the Overseas Citizen of India program since its inception, eliminating what NRIs had long considered one of its most frustrating requirements. As of April 8, 2026, applicants no longer need to complete six months of continuous stay in India before filing an OCI application from within the country. Under the old rules, foreign nationals of Indian origin who were visiting India had to remain in the country for at least six months before they could apply — a requirement that was impractical for working professionals and families who could not take extended leave.

Under the revised framework, applicants need only hold a valid long-term visa and the required supporting documents to submit their application soon after arrival in India. Tourist, missionary, mountaineering and e-visa holders remain ineligible to apply from within India.

New Fee Structure

The fee revision, effective April 1, 2026, consolidates and simplifies the cost structure. A fresh OCI application costs $275 when filed outside India through Indian missions and authorized VFS Global centers, payable in equivalent local currency. For applications filed within India, the fee is ₹15,000 via demand draft to the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The more significant savings come on reissuance. Updating an OCI card due to changes in personal details or reaching the mandatory re-issuance age of 20 costs just $25 outside India. A duplicate card for loss or damage costs $100. An ICWF surcharge of $3 applies to all fees paid abroad.

Strict New Passport Update Compliance

The overhaul comes with a new compliance obligation that all OCI cardholders should note. Every time an OCI holder receives a new foreign passport, they must update their OCI record within 90 days. The update itself is free when completed within the window — it requires uploading the new passport's bio page and a recent photograph through the OCI Miscellaneous Services portal, with no physical visit needed.

Miss the 90-day deadline, however, and the otherwise free update becomes a paid process with a $25 penalty. Immigration law firm Fragomen noted that some travelers have already been asked to show proof of the update at Delhi and Bengaluru immigration counters, suggesting enforcement has begun in earnest.

Digital e-OCI Goes Live

In a parallel modernization move announced on May 6, India introduced an electronic OCI card option. Eligible foreign nationals can now obtain an e-OCI through the ociservices.gov.in portal, with the physical card becoming optional rather than mandatory. The digital system supports e-signing of declarations and real-time tracking of application status.

The shift to digital is linked to upgraded biometric verification systems being deployed at Indian airports. The e-OCI will enable faster "e-gate" immigration processing by matching passport and OCI data in real time — a meaningful improvement for frequent travelers who have long endured manual document checks at Indian ports of entry.

Broader Eligibility for Sri Lankan Tamils

The revised rules also expand eligibility for the Sri Lankan Indian Tamil diaspora. Fifth- and sixth-generation persons of Indian origin from Sri Lanka can now apply for OCI cards, extending the previous limit of fourth-generation descendants. The change is particularly significant for communities with limited historical documentation, opening a pathway to Indian diaspora status for a broader group that has maintained cultural ties across generations.

Marriage and Child Application Rules Tightened

For OCI applications based on marriage to an Indian citizen or existing OCI cardholder, the marriage must now be registered and must have subsisted for at least two years before the date of application. Applications for children born abroad require apostille-certified documents, adding a layer of verification that immigration attorneys say aligns with broader global trends in document authentication.

What OCI Holders Should Do Now

The immediate action item for the estimated 4 million OCI cardholders worldwide is straightforward: check whether your passport details are current on the OCI portal. If you have received a new passport and have not updated your OCI record, the 90-day clock may already be ticking. The penalty is modest at $25, but the risk of complications at immigration counters is real. For those considering a new OCI application, the removal of the six-month stay rule means applications can be filed during shorter visits to India, substantially reducing the logistical burden.

nri_angle: The removal of the six-month stay requirement is a direct quality-of-life improvement for NRIs who can now file OCI applications during shorter visits to India.
